Why AI detectors flag human writing as AI

A high AI score on something you wrote yourself is unsettling. It is also common, and the reasons are well understood.

Published 17 November 2026

Detectors measure style, not authorship

No detector can see who typed a text. Each one measures features of the writing and compares them with what it has learned about human and machine text. Two features do most of the work. The first is predictability: how unsurprising each word is given the words before it. The second is variation, often called burstiness: how much sentence length and structure change through the passage. Machine text tends to be predictable and even. So does a lot of careful human writing.

The kinds of human writing that get flagged

  • Formal and academic prose. Abstracts, literature reviews and reports follow conventions: measured sentences, no contractions, standard connecting phrases. Those conventions are exactly what language models learned to imitate.
  • Writing in a second language. Writers using English as an additional language often rely on a smaller, safer vocabulary and on phrases learned as fixed units. Research on detectors has repeatedly found that such writing is misclassified more often than writing by native speakers.
  • Heavily edited text. Grammar tools and several rounds of polishing remove the small irregularities that mark a text as human.
  • Short passages. A few sentences give a detector very little to measure, so the result is close to a guess.
  • Formulaic genres. Cover letters, product descriptions and instructions sound alike whoever writes them.

What to do if your own work is flagged

First, look at why. A detector that explains itself, such as the one on this site, lists the signals that raised the score and the sentences involved. Often the cause is a run of same-length sentences or a cluster of stock phrases, and you can decide whether those are worth changing for the reader’s sake.

Second, keep evidence of your process. Drafts, notes, version history in your word processor, and the sources you read are far stronger evidence of authorship than any score. If you are asked about a piece of work, offer those and offer to discuss the content.

Third, do not rewrite good prose just to move a number. Detectors disagree with one another, and a text adjusted to satisfy one can still be flagged by the next.

If you are the one checking

Treat a score as a reason to look closer, never as a finding. A false accusation does real harm, and every detector produces false positives. Ask about the writing process, compare with the person’s earlier work, and follow your institution’s procedure. Most detector makers, including this one, say plainly that a score must not be the sole basis for a decision about a person.
